Downloading and caching BODS GTFS data

bods-gtfs-caching.Rmd
library(bodsr2)

Introduction

The Bus Open Data Service (BODS) provides timetable data for bus services in England as regional GTFS zip files. These files are large — the East Midlands zip is around 600MB — and downloading one on every session would be impractical.

bodsr2 solves this with a simple caching layer. The first call to gtfs_load() downloads the zip, parses it into a tidytransit object, and saves it to a local cache. Subsequent calls load directly from the cache, which is dramatically faster.

Loading GTFS data 

library(bodsr2)

gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands")
#> ℹ Downloading GTFS data for "east_midlands" from BODS.
#> ℹ This file is large and may take a moment.
#> ✔ Zip saved to ~/.cache/R/bodsr2/east_midlands.zip
#> ℹ Reading GTFS zip for "east_midlands". This may take a moment.
#> ✔ GTFS data cached to ~/.cache/R/bodsr2/east_midlands.rds

On a typical connection this takes around 40 seconds. The second call is much faster:

gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands")
# completes in around 3 seconds

The cache is stored in your platform’s user cache directory. You can find it with gtfs_cache_dir(), and clear it with gtfs_delete_cache("east_midlands").

The cache is automatically refreshed when the GTFS feed expires (indicated by feed_end_date in the feed info). You can also force a fresh download at any time:

gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands", download = TRUE)

What’s in the object

gtfs_load() returns a tidygtfs object — a named list of tibbles, one for each GTFS table:

names(gtfs)
#>  [1] "agency"         "stops"          "routes"         "calendar"      
#>  [5] "calendar_dates" "trips"          "shapes"         "feed_info"     
#>  [9] "stop_times"

This is a standard tidytransit object. See the tidytransit documentation for a full guide to working with it. The rest of this vignette shows one example to illustrate the kind of analysis the object supports.

Example: services departing from Derby Bus Station Bay 4

The V1 Villager service (Derby to Burton-upon-Trent) departs from Bay 4 at Derby Bus Station. Its stop ID in the GTFS data is "1090BSTN04":

gtfs$stops |>
  dplyr::filter(stop_id == "1090BSTN04") |>
  dplyr::select(stop_id, stop_name, platform_code)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   stop_id    stop_name   platform_code
#>   <chr>      <chr>       <chr>        
#> 1 1090BSTN04 Bus Station 4

To find all services that start from this stop, we look for trips where this stop appears at the lowest stop sequence number:

library(dplyr)

gtfs$stop_times |>
  filter(stop_id == "1090BSTN04") |>
  left_join(gtfs$trips, by = "trip_id") |>
  left_join(gtfs$routes, by = "route_id") |>
  distinct(route_short_name, trip_headsign)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   route_short_name trip_headsign            
#>   <chr>            <chr>                    
#> 1 V1               Derby Bus Station        
#> 2 V1               Burton                   
#> 3 V1               Burton Train Stn         
#> 4 TP               Derby Bus Station (Bay 4)
#> 5 70               Derby Bus Station        
#> 6 70A              Derby Bus Station        
#> 7 70A              Methodist Church         
#> 8 V1               Wetmore                  
#> 9 70A              Willington

Four routes use Bay 4: the V1, TP, 70, and 70A. The trip_headsign column shows the destination as displayed on the front of the bus, which is more informative than route_long_name (not always populated in BODS GTFS data). The V1 entries include both outbound trips (to Burton and Wetmore) and inbound trips terminating at Derby Bus Station, since Bay 4 serves as both the origin and terminus for this route.
